terms.gloss: knock, bump (a part of the body, or someone)
evidence: Quint. 6.3.67: caput … ad fornicem Fabium offendisse
Plaut. Curc. 282: nē quem … capite … offendam
terms.comment: The part of the body is the object, with ad and what it hits (caput, pedem offendere); or the person bumped is the object and the part of the body is in the ablative (Plaut. Curc. 282).

terms.register: plērumque poētica; in Cicerōnis ōrātiōne solūtā nōn invenītur (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: nē quem in cursū capite aut cubitō aut pectore offendam aut genū
phrases.english: so that I don’t bump into anyone with my head or elbow or chest or knee as I run

phrases.latin: caput eum ad fornicem Fabium offendisse
phrases.english: that he had hit his head on the Arch of Fabius (Cicero’s joke about a very tall man)

phrases.latin: In manibus portābunt tē, nē forte offendās ad lapidem pedem tuum.
phrases.english: They will carry you in their hands, so that you do not strike your foot against a stone.
Mind you don’t bump your head.

sources: Lewis & Short: offendo · Lewis & Short: illido
